metaData.title: Everyone Is Paying for the $700 Billion Bill
metaData.oneSentenceSummary: This article deeply analyzes the chain reaction triggered by the $700 billion AI capital expenditure of the Silicon Valley Seven, revealing how it squeezes chip capacity, drives up storage prices, competes with communities for electricity, and uses financial instruments like SPVs to layer risks onto ordinary consumers and the public.
metaData.summary: This is the third article in the "AI Faith and Bubble" series, focusing on the systemic impact of the Silicon Valley Seven's projected $700 billion AI capital expenditure in 2026. The article unfolds on three levels: First, the supply chain level, where consumer electronics giants like Apple, Xiaomi, and Huawei are under pressure as TSMC's capacity is squeezed by AI computing power vendors like NVIDIA and storage prices surge, forcing them to raise prices or cut product lines, with profit distribution heavily skewed. Second, the energy level, where the surging electricity demand from AI data centers conflicts with aging grid infrastructure. Tech giants are building their own power plants and competing for electricity, leading to higher residential electricity bills and triggering environmental and community issues. Third, the financial level, where tech giants use off-balance-sheet financing tools like SPVs and REITs to transfer debt risks to external capital such as pension funds and insurance companies, creating an artificial financial asset pipeline with risks layered and hidden. The article cites warnings from industry insiders, research institutions, and Michael Burry, the real-life inspiration for "The Big Short," revealing the structural risks and cost socialization behind the AI boom.

mainPoints.point: AI capital expenditure squeezes advanced process capacity, forcing consumer electronics giants to raise prices or cut product lines.
mainPoints.explanation: NVIDIA and other AI computing power vendors have bought up TSMC's advanced capacity, causing Apple to lose its top customer status. Xiaomi and Huawei face soaring storage prices (DRAM up over 50%, NAND up over 90%), leading to the discontinuation of entry-level phones and flagship prices breaking the 10,000 yuan mark.

mainPoints.point: The electricity demand of AI data centers is severely mismatched with grid infrastructure, with costs passed on to residents.
mainPoints.explanation: The global total capacity of AI data centers has reached 30 GW, with an annual electricity consumption of 262.8 billion kWh. Tech giants are building their own power plants and competing for electricity, causing residential electricity bills to rise (e.g., Memphis households see an increase of $12-15 per month) and triggering environmental lawsuits and community conflicts.

mainPoints.point: Tech giants use off-balance-sheet financing tools like SPVs and REITs to transfer AI infrastructure risks to pension funds and insurance companies.
mainPoints.explanation: Meta, xAI, and others have raised over $120 billion through SPVs without the debt appearing on their balance sheets. Data center REITs package long-term lease contracts for public listing, allowing external capital to bear the risks. Michael Burry warns this is a "scam," with risks layered and hidden.

keyQuotes: All financial crises, in the final analysis, are a resonance of human nature and institutions. History does not repeat itself exactly, but it always rhymes.
No matter how many warnings are issued or how many regulations are enacted, people will always find new ways to believe that good times never end; people will always package hope as certainty.

It takes only 8-12 complex steps to erase hundreds of billions of dollars worth of NVIDIA GPUs from the balance sheet. Each step is legal, each step is disclosed. But the entire structure's purpose is to move credit risk off the balance sheet, removing it from observable market pricing.

relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: Based on SpaceX's prospectus, this article analyzes its $45 billion computing contract with Anthropic, its holdings of 18,712 Bitcoin, its board composition and aggressive governance structure, and the critical significance of the V3 Starship test flight for its valuation.

relatedArticles.title: Why Did Hermes Take Over from OpenClaw in Just Two Months?
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: This article provides an in-depth comparison between the rising open-source AI Agent star Hermes and its predecessor OpenClaw, arguing that Hermes' success stems not from functional superiority but from encapsulating decision complexity—such as skill auto-evolution and proactive memory management—within underlying deterministic rules. This engineering safety net allowed it to deliver an automated 'gets better with use' experience precisely when the underlying technology was just barely sufficient.
